Text | Zhihan Guo

Editors | Fanyu Meng, Er Mu

In the previous article (How can we tell how far away a sound is?), we saw that auditory signals contain cues that let us judge how far away a sound source is. This article takes one of those cues, the initial time delay gap, as an example and shows how to design a listening test that investigates its role in binaural distance perception. A listening test generally has three main parts: the theoretical background, the test preparation (measurements and programming), and the analysis of the results. Let’s go through them step by step.

1. The initial time delay gap


The room impulse response is a property of a room: it describes the transfer function between a sound source and a microphone. It can be divided into three parts: the direct sound, the early reflections and the reverberation. The initial time delay gap (ITDG) is the interval between the direct sound and the first sound reflected from a surface, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1: Schematic of a room impulse response

Some researchers regard the ITDG as a distance cue. Stephan Werner and Simone Füg showed that changing the length of the ITDG can alter perceived distance [1]. As Figure 2 illustrates, when the microphone position is fixed, the farther away the source, the smaller the path difference between the direct sound and the first reflection, and therefore the shorter the ITDG. This led to the hypothesis that modifying the ITDG could influence binaural distance perception. Note, however, that the hypothesis holds only when the floor is the sole reflecting surface, as in a hemi-anechoic chamber or a fairly empty room; objects between the source and the microphone alter the first reflection and so undermine it. Other researchers disagree altogether: in his experiments, Fotis Georgiou found that the ITDG does not appear to be a salient cue for distance perception [2].

Figure 2: The ITDG when only the floor reflection is considered, where dD denotes the direct path and dR the path of the first reflection

2. Experimental design

2.1 Measuring binaural room impulse responses (BRIRs)

To investigate the role of the ITDG in distance perception with binaural audio, we first had to build a database of BRIRs (binaural room impulse responses). BRIRs were measured with a dummy head (also called an artificial head) and swept-sine signals in two rooms at Chalmers University of Technology, labeled EH and LR. They were measured at four azimuths (0°, 30°, 60° and 90°) at distances of 2 m, 4 m, 6 m and 8 m. To make sure a usable ITDG could be obtained, any objects between the source and the microphone were removed during the measurements. All measured BRIRs were then processed with fade-in and fade-out windows. In an ideal measurement environment such as a hemi-anechoic chamber, with the dummy head and source at a height of 1.6 m, the ITDG curve should resemble the ideal curve in Figure 3. We processed the impulse responses measured at the dummy head’s left and right ears in EH and LR and extracted the ITDG data, and found that the measurements matched the ideal curve. To keep things simple, this study used the left-ear impulse response as the basis for further analysis and modification.

Figure 3: The ITDG curve at a height of 1.6 m when only the floor reflection is considered, with measured data from EH and LR

2.2 How the ITDG was modified

The core idea of the modification algorithm is to adjust the ITDG length of a given impulse response (say, the BRIR at 2 m and 30°) so that it produces the same perceived distance as a BRIR at some other distance and the same angle (say, the BRIR at 6 m and 30°). If this approach proves effective, the response over an entire area could be represented by measuring only a handful of BRIRs. To this end, each measured impulse response was split into three parts: the direct part (from the start of the impulse to 1 ms after the direct-sound peak), the early-reflection part (the 35 ms after the direct part) and the reverberant part (from the end of the early-reflection part to the end of the signal). These parts are shown in Figure 4.

Figure 4: The impulse response before and after ITDG modification. Because this study treats only the floor reflection as a distance cue, a spurious peak appears in the measured impulse response.

To pinpoint the onset of the first reflection from the floor and rule out spurious peaks within the ITDG, the measured BRIRs were analyzed with an improved kurtosis-based algorithm combined with the ideal ITDG curve [3]. To simplify matters further, the modification gave priority to the ear nearer the source: the amount by which the right ear was modified was tied directly to the left ear, since the left ear was always closer to the source in these measurements. For example, when the left-ear ITDG was shortened by 1 ms, the right-ear ITDG was shortened by the same amount. The direct and reverberant parts were left unchanged, while the early-reflection part overlapping the ITDG was compressed or stretched to obtain the ITDG required for the target distance. Because the modified section is tiny compared with the BRIR as a whole, any resulting changes in sound pressure level and spectral characteristics were considered negligible.

2.3 Test procedure

The experiment set out to determine whether modifying the ITDG affects auditory distance perception in different scenarios. Two factors were studied: target distance (2 m or 6 m) and audio material (speech or drums). Since the BRIRs were measured in two rooms, this gave 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 trials in total. The listening test was modeled on MUSHRA [4] but was not identical to it; for example, it had no anchor. MUSHRA is a very widely used method in audio testing. Note that its Chinese version contains some translation errors, so we recommend consulting another language version. The test program was built with MATLAB App Designer; its interface is shown in Figure 5. Each trial had three reference stimuli and four test stimuli. The references were produced by convolving the audio material with the measured BRIRs. The four options were ref, orig, drr and drr+itdg. All references and options were loudness-matched to exclude the influence of loudness on distance perception.

Take one trial as an example. Here the target distance is 6 m, the modified BRIR comes from 2 m, the measurements come from the entrance hall, and the material is speech. The options are as follows:

ref: identical to the reference at 6 m

orig: identical to the reference at 2 m

drr: the BRIR at 2 m, adjusted only so that its direct-to-reverberant energy ratio (DRR) matches that of the BRIR at 6 m, with the ITDG unchanged.

drr+itdg: the ITDG of the BRIR at 2 m is changed to match that at 6 m using the method described above; then, with the direct part left unchanged, the amplitude of the remaining parts is adjusted until the DRR matches that of the BRIR at 6 m.

Note that the four options were presented in random order, so participants could not guess which stimulus was which.

Figure 5: The interface of the listening test program

3. Results


Because the experiment was demanding, five participants took part. All were experienced in listening tests and reported no hearing impairments. To check the accuracy of the results, we followed the MUSHRA post-screening method, adapted to the compressive nature of human distance perception: a participant’s results were to be excluded if, in more than 15% of all trials, they rated the hidden reference more than 10% away from the true distance (that is, outside 1.8–2.2 m for 2 m, or outside 5.4–6.6 m for 6 m). All participants passed this screening, so their results were considered valid.

The results are presented as violin plots, which combine a density curve and a box plot in a single display and make the distribution of the data easier to read. The overall results (Figure 6) show that the medians of ref and orig match the actual measured distances, which confirms that the experimental results are reliable. Further analysis shows that both drr and drr+itdg produce a sense of distance similar to the target, but drr+itdg brings no systematic improvement over drr. To understand the results in more depth, we analyzed the data statistically. Because there were few participants and the MUSHRA results were not normally distributed (see ref and orig, for example), non-parametric tests were used.

Figure 6: Overall results of the listening test

A Friedman test found the differences across all trials to be significant at p<0.05. Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were therefore run as post hoc tests, with Bonferroni–Holm correction of the p-values; the results are shown in Figure 7. Orig differs clearly from ref, drr and drr+itdg, but there are no significant differences among drr, drr+itdg and ref. This suggests that the ITDG does not play a very important role in distance perception, which agrees with Georgiou’s conclusion [2].

Figure 7: Bonferroni–Holm corrected p-values for all pairwise comparisons, pooling the speech and drum stimuli and the near and far references. A blue background marks a significant difference at p<0.05.

4. Conclusion

This article set out to explore the role of the ITDG in distance perception with binaural audio. We measured binaural room impulse responses in two rooms at Chalmers University of Technology, modified them, and studied how the ITDG affects perceived distance. The results show that although modifying the ITDG can change perceived distance in binaural audio, the effect was not significant in this experiment. This suggests that the ITDG may not be a major cue for distance perception.

Note that the conclusions of this study apply only when the floor is the sole reflecting surface, as in a hemi-anechoic chamber or a fairly empty room. In real environments there may be several objects between the source and the listening position, which affect the first reflection and the usefulness of the ITDG. Moreover, because the ITDG is not itself a binaural cue, modifying it involved many simplifications, and the resulting errors may also have influenced the results. Future research may therefore need to examine further how the ITDG affects distance perception in more complex environments.

References

[1] Werner, S., & Füg, S. (2012, November). Controlled Auditory Distance Perception using Binaural Headphone Reproduction–Evaluation via Listening Tests. In Proceedings of the 27th Tonmeistertagung, VDT International Convention, Cologne, Germany (pp. 22-25).

[2] F. Georgiou, RELATIVE DISTANCE PERCEPTION OF SOUND SOURCES IN CRITICAL LISTENING ENVIRONMENT VIA BINAURAL REPRODUCTION. PhD thesis, 09 2012.

[3] Usher, J. (2010). An improved method to determine the onset timings of reflections in an acoustic impulse response. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 127(4), EL172-EL177.

[4] International Telecommunication Union. (2015). Method for the subjective assessment of intermediate quality level of audio systems (ITU-R BS.1116-3). https://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-BS.1116-3-201502-I/en
